cards.title: Git Object Model (Blob, Tree, Commit, Tag)
cards.question: Explain Git Object Model (Blob, Tree, Commit, Tag)
cards.answer_30s: Git is a content-addressable filesystem where every object is keyed by its SHA-1/SHA-256 hash. Blobs store file contents; Trees store directory structures and filenames; Commits point to a root Tree, parent commit(s), and author metadata; Branches are simply 41-byte files pointing to a commit hash.

code.body:
git cat-file -p HEAD
git rev-parse HEAD

cards.typical_use: Understanding why branching, switching, and verifying history integrity are nearly instant.
pitfalls: Because branches are just lightweight pointers, deleting a merged branch does not delete commits.

cards.title: Merge vs Rebase vs Squash
cards.question: Explain Merge vs Rebase vs Squash
cards.answer_30s: `git merge` creates a merge commit preserving true branching chronology. `git rebase` replays your feature commits onto a new base commit for a clean linear history. `git merge --squash` collapses a messy feature branch into a single commit on main.

code.body:
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

cards.typical_use: Keeping team commit history readable and bisectable.
pitfalls: Golden Rule of Rebasing: NEVER rebase commits that have already been pushed to a shared public branch.

cards.title: Reset (Soft, Mixed, Hard) vs Revert
cards.question: Explain Reset (Soft, Mixed, Hard) vs Revert
cards.answer_30s: `git reset` moves the branch pointer backward: `--soft` keeps changes staged, `--mixed` (default) keeps them in working dir unstaged, `--hard` discards all changes. `git revert` creates a NEW inverse commit, safely undoing changes on shared branches without rewriting history.
cards.typical_use: Safely rolling back bad merges on main vs tidying local unpushed commits.
pitfalls: Use `git revert` on shared branches (`main`); use `git reset` only on local unpushed work.

cards.title: Git Reflog & Disaster Recovery
cards.question: Explain Git Reflog & Disaster Recovery
cards.answer_30s: Git records every movement of HEAD and branch tips locally in the reflog (default retention 90 days). Even after a bad `git reset --hard` or botched rebase, you can recover lost commits by checking `git reflog` and resetting or branching back to the old SHA.

code.body:
git reflog
git checkout -b recovered-work HEAD@{2}

cards.typical_use: Recovering 'lost' commits after an accidental hard reset or rebase.
pitfalls: Note that reflog is strictly local—uncommitted changes that were never `git add`/`git commit`-ted cannot be recovered from reflog.

cards.title: Git Bisect for Binary-Searching Regressions
cards.question: Explain Git Bisect for Binary-Searching Regressions
cards.answer_30s: `git bisect` performs O(log N) binary search across commit history to pinpoint the exact commit that introduced a bug, and can even run an automated test script via `git bisect run`.

code.body:
git bisect start
git bisect bad HEAD
git bisect good v1.4.0
git bisect run pytest tests/test_auth.py

cards.typical_use: Isolating subtle regressions across hundreds of commits in minutes.
pitfalls: Clean, atomic, passing commits make `git bisect` dramatically more effective.

cards.title: Interactive Rebase, Cherry-Pick & Stash
cards.question: Explain Interactive Rebase, Cherry-Pick & Stash
cards.answer_30s: `git rebase -i` lets you reorder, squash, fixup, reword, or drop local commits before opening a PR. `git cherry-pick` copies a specific commit (e.g., a hotfix) onto another branch. `git stash` temporarily shelves uncommitted work.
cards.typical_use: Preparing clean PRs and backporting urgent fixes to release branches.
pitfalls: Use `git push --force-with-lease` instead of `--force` after rebasing a PR branch so you don't overwrite a teammate's commits.

cards.title: Q: What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
cards.question: Q: What is the difference between `git fetch` and `git pull`?
cards.answer_30s: A: `git fetch` downloads remote commits and updates remote-tracking refs (`origin/main`) without touching your working directory or local branch. `git pull` runs `git fetch` followed immediately by `git merge` (or `git rebase` with `--rebase`).
pitfalls: Using `git fetch` first lets you inspect incoming changes (`git diff HEAD..origin/main`) before integrating.

cards.title: Q: Why use `git push --force-with-lease` instead of `git push --force`?
cards.question: Q: Why use `git push --force-with-lease` instead of `git push --force`?
cards.answer_30s: A: `--force` unconditionally overwrites the remote branch, destroying any commits pushed by teammates since your last fetch. `--force-with-lease` aborts if the remote branch tip doesn't match what you expect locally.
cards.typical_use: Safe force-pushing after interactive rebases on PR branches.

cards.title: Q: What is a Detached HEAD state and how do you fix it?
cards.question: Q: What is a Detached HEAD state and how do you fix it?
cards.answer_30s: A: Detached HEAD means HEAD points directly to a commit SHA rather than a branch name (common after `git checkout <sha>` or tag). Commits made there aren't on any branch and will eventually be garbage-collected unless you create a branch with `git switch -c fix-branch`.
cards.typical_use: Recovering work committed while inspecting an old tag or commit.
pitfalls: Creating a branch immediately saves all commits made in detached HEAD.

cards.title: Q: How do you remove a secret or huge binary accidentally committed to Git?
cards.question: Q: How do you remove a secret or huge binary accidentally committed to Git?
cards.answer_30s: A: Simply deleting the file in a new commit leaves the secret in Git history. You must rewrite history across all commits using `git filter-repo` (replacing legacy filter-branch/BFG), force-push, and MOST IMPORTANTLY rotate/revoke the leaked secret immediately.
cards.typical_use: Security incident response for leaked API keys.
pitfalls: Interviewers test whether you remember step #1: rotate the credential immediately—history rewriting alone doesn't un-leak a pushed key.

cards.title: Q: Trunk-Based Development vs GitFlow — when do you use each?
cards.question: Q: Trunk-Based Development vs GitFlow — when do you use each?
cards.answer_30s: A: Trunk-Based Development uses short-lived feature branches merged daily into `main` with CI/CD and feature flags—ideal for SaaS/web teams shipping continuously. GitFlow uses long-lived `develop`, `release`, and `hotfix` branches—better suited for versioned, packaged, or regulated software with scheduled releases.

code.body: # Trunk-based: short branches + feature flags + automated CI gates

cards.typical_use: Engineering workflow and CI/CD culture question.
pitfalls: Trunk-based development correlates strongly with higher deployment frequency and fewer merge conflicts.

cards.title: Q: How do you resolve a complex merge conflict cleanly?
cards.question: Q: How do you resolve a complex merge conflict cleanly?
cards.answer_30s: A: Inspect conflict markers (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`), understand both intents (`git log -p -n 3`), resolve manually or via 3-way merge tool (`git mergetool`), run the test suite, and complete with `git add` + `git commit` (or `git rebase --continue`). Enable `git rerere` to auto-reuse resolutions.
cards.typical_use: Handling long-lived branch conflicts and repetitive rebases.
pitfalls: Mentioning `git rerere` (Reuse Recorded Resolution) is a pro tip interviewers love.

cards.title: Q: How do `git diff`, `git diff --staged`, and `git diff main...HEAD` differ?
cards.question: Q: How do `git diff`, `git diff --staged`, and `git diff main...HEAD` differ?
cards.answer_30s: A: `git diff` compares working tree vs staging area (index). `git diff --staged` compares staging area vs HEAD. Triple-dot `main...HEAD` shows changes on your branch since it diverged from `main` (the exact PR diff), whereas double-dot `main..HEAD` compares the two tips directly.
pitfalls: GitHub/GitLab PR diffs use triple-dot (`...`) semantics.

cards.title: Q: How do you revert a bad merge commit?
cards.question: Q: How do you revert a bad merge commit?
cards.answer_30s: A: A merge commit has two parents, so `git revert <merge-sha>` requires `-m 1` to specify which parent (`1` = mainline target branch) to keep. Note that reverting a merge doesn't erase the feature commits, so if you re-merge the same branch later you must revert the revert first.
cards.typical_use: Emergency production rollback after merging a broken PR.
pitfalls: Knowing the `-m 1` flag and the 'revert the revert' gotcha is a classic senior Git question.
